# Memo: Local AI Hardware Expansion vs. Utilisation Improvement

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** Compute capacity decision for local AI workloads

## Context

We are approaching a decision point on AI compute capacity. Our current local hardware is running at moderate utilisation during business hours with significant idle capacity overnight and on weekends. Meanwhile, demand for inference and fine-tuning work is growing, and two teams have flagged latency-sensitive applications that our current setup handles adequately but not comfortably. The question before us is whether to purchase additional hardware now or to invest in squeezing more out of what we already own. This memo lays out the trade-offs and offers a recommendation.

## The case for improving utilisation first

The strongest argument for optimisation is that it is nearly free money. Our GPUs sit idle roughly sixty percent of the calendar week. Even modest gains through better scheduling, batching inference requests, and shifting batch workloads like fine-tuning runs into overnight windows could effectively give us the equivalent of one or two additional accelerators without capital expenditure. The engineering effort involved is not trivial, but it is a known quantity: a job scheduler upgrade, some queueing discipline, and discipline from teams about when they submit work.

Latency considerations cut in both directions here. Consolidating workloads onto fewer devices can increase contention and tail latency for interactive applications, which is precisely what our latency-sensitive teams care about. However, better batching and smarter routing often *reduce* p99 latency for inference even on shared hardware, because requests spend less time waiting in inefficient queues. The latency question is empirical, not a priori, and we should measure it before assuming either direction.

Reliability also favours utilisation work in one respect: it does not add new hardware to maintain, power, cool, or eventually decommission. On the other hand, running equipment closer to thermal and scheduling limits can expose latent failure modes. Our current comfortable margins may be quietly absorbing variability that tighter packing would surface.

## The case for buying hardware

The utilisation argument has a ceiling. Even perfect scheduling cannot create capacity at 2pm on a Tuesday if demand genuinely exceeds supply at that moment. If our peak-hour demand is real and growing, optimisation buys us months, not years. Hardware lead times remain non-trivial, so deciding to buy later means feeling the crunch later but ordering later too.

There is also an opportunity cost to deferral that is easy to underweight. Every week that teams wait for fine-tuning slots or work around inference congestion is a week of slower product iteration. That cost is diffuse and hard to measure, which is exactly why it tends to be ignored in capacity planning. Against this stands the opportunity cost of capital tied up in hardware that might sit underused if demand forecasts prove optimistic, or if model efficiency improvements (quantisation, distillation, smaller models matching larger ones) reduce our per-task compute needs faster than demand grows.

Reversibility is where the two options differ most sharply. Utilisation work is highly reversible and highly composable: every scheduling improvement we make remains valuable whether or not we later buy hardware, because it will improve the efficiency of the new machines too. Nothing is wasted. A hardware purchase, by contrast, is largely irreversible. Depreciation begins immediately, resale value for AI accelerators is volatile, and the wrong spec for a fast-moving ecosystem is a multi-year mistake. This asymmetry matters. When two options are close on expected value, prefer the one that keeps future options open.

## Uncertainty

We should be honest that our demand forecast is soft. Two teams' projections drive most of the expected growth, and both have historically overestimated. Model efficiency is also moving quickly in our favour. These uncertainties argue for a decision structure that hedges rather than a single bet.

## Recommendation

We recommend a sequenced approach. Commit now to the utilisation work: scheduler upgrades, overnight batch scheduling, and inference batching, with a target of raising effective peak capacity within six to eight weeks. In parallel, specify the hardware we would buy and get quotes, so that if measured peak demand still exceeds capacity after optimisation lands, we can order with minimal additional delay. Set an explicit decision checkpoint at the end of the optimisation window, with agreed thresholds: if optimised utilisation at peak still exceeds roughly eighty-five percent, or if latency-sensitive workloads miss their targets, we buy.

This path captures the cheap capacity first, preserves the option to buy with little lost time, and forces us to replace speculation with measurement before committing capital. It is the reversible move, taken first, with the irreversible move held ready.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** Local AI Hardware Expansion vs. Improved Utilisation of Existing Capacity

We've been asked to decide whether to purchase additional local AI hardware or to invest our limited engineering time in squeezing more out of the machines we already own. This memo lays out the tradeoffs as I see them and closes with a recommendation. My aim is not to pretend there is a risk-free path, but to identify which risks are cheaper to be wrong about.

Let's start with the current situation. Our existing GPU nodes are, by most measurements, underutilised. Average utilisation hovers in the thirties, and even at peak we rarely saturate memory or interconnect. That gap is partly a scheduling problem: batch sizes are conservative, jobs are pinned to specific nodes out of habit rather than topology, and our inference stack doesn't aggregate requests across services. In other words, a meaningful fraction of the capacity we're considering buying is already sitting in the rack, unclaimed.

The purchase path is seductive because it is simple. New hardware arrives, capacity concerns recede, and no one has to refactor a scheduler. But it carries real costs beyond the invoice. Capital expenditure on accelerators is front-loaded and unforgiving; the same generation of silicon that feels cutting-edge today will be mid-tier within eighteen months, and its resale value decays accordingly. There are also the quieter costs: rack space, power and cooling headroom, spares, and the operational burden of maintaining a larger fleet with the same number of people. And there is opportunity cost in the most literal sense. Money spent on hardware is money not available for the software work that would benefit every workload we run, present and future.

The utilisation path is the mirror image. Its costs are mostly in engineering time and in the patience required to see results. Its benefits compound: better batching, smarter placement, and shared serving improve latency for everyone, not just the workloads that happen to land on new silicon. Latency deserves special mention here. Adding hardware can reduce queueing delay, but it does nothing for per-request latency, which is dominated by kernel efficiency, memory bandwidth, and how well we overlap compute with data movement. If our users are feeling slowness at the individual-request level, more GPUs will not fix that; better software will. Conversely, if the pain is throughput and queue depth, utilisation work helps first and hardware helps second.

Reliability cuts in an interesting direction. A larger fleet offers redundancy on paper, but redundancy only materialises if we have the operational maturity to fail over gracefully. Right now we don't fully trust our own failover, which means new nodes would initially add surface area for things to go wrong faster than they add genuine resilience. Utilisation work forces us to confront scheduling, health checking, and graceful degradation, which are precisely the capabilities that make any future hardware investment safer. In that sense the two paths are not entirely alternatives; the software path de-risks the hardware path.

Reversibility is, to me, the decisive consideration. Utilisation improvements are almost entirely reversible and portable: better scheduling logic, request coalescing, and quantisation choices can be tuned, rolled back, or carried forward to whatever hardware we own next. A hardware purchase is largely irreversible once the capital is committed, and its value erodes on a predictable curve. When two options have comparable expected benefit, the one that is cheaper to unwind is the one to prefer, because our forecasts are least reliable exactly where the stakes are highest. Demand for local inference is genuinely uncertain; it could double next quarter if the planned product features land, or it could stall if they slip. Betting irreversibly on the optimistic branch is imprudent when a reversible investment captures most of the same upside.

So my recommendation is this: commit the next quarter to utilisation work, with concrete targets, and defer the hardware decision until we can measure demand against a well-run fleet. If, after batching and placement improvements, we are still saturating capacity at peak, that is strong evidence for purchase, and we will buy with better information and better software to exploit it. If utilisation gains absorb the projected load, we will have saved the capital and built durable capabilities.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. It is possible that demand grows faster than software improvements can keep pace, and in that case we will feel some pain while the purchase order clears. I accept that risk because it is bounded and temporary, whereas the risk of overbuying is permanent. The team should treat this not as a rejection of hardware but as a sequencing decision: earn the purchase with evidence. I'm confident this is the right order of operations, and I'm happy to revisit the moment the data says otherwise.

**Memo: On AI Hardware Procurement vs. Utilisation Improvement**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Date:** Internal
**Re:** Whether to purchase additional local AI accelerators or invest in better utilisation of existing capacity

---

We currently face a decision that many small teams encounter at some point: our local AI hardware is feeling constrained, and the instinctive response is to buy more of it. Before committing capital, however, I want us to think carefully about whether the bottleneck is genuinely a shortage of silicon or a shortage of discipline in how we use what we already own. My recommendation, stated up front, is that we spend the next quarter on utilisation improvements and defer any hardware purchase, revisiting procurement only if measured demand still exceeds capacity after those improvements land.

Let me start with cost, since it is the most visible factor. New accelerators carry not just the purchase price but the full lifecycle burden: power, cooling, rack space, maintenance contracts, and the engineering time to integrate and babysit them. For a team of our size, that total cost of ownership is substantial relative to our budget, and it is largely irreversible once incurred. Depreciating hardware that sits idle is the worst of both worlds. By contrast, utilisation work—better scheduling, batching of inference requests, quantisation of models where quality permits, and consolidating workloads that currently run on separate devices—costs mostly engineering time, which we already pay for, and produces knowledge that retains value regardless of what hardware we own in the future.

Latency deserves equal attention, because it is where the two paths genuinely diverge. If our workloads are latency-sensitive—interactive tools, real-time assistance, anything a human waits on—then raw spare capacity does matter, since queuing delays compound quickly as utilisation approaches saturation. But it is worth being honest about what our actual latency profile looks like. Much of our current slowness, on my reading of the situation, stems from poor batching and models running at higher precision than the use case requires, not from exhausted hardware. Fixing those is cheaper and faster than procurement lead times, which currently run to months for the class of hardware we would consider. If, after tuning, we still see p95 latencies that hurt the product, that is real evidence for buying.

Reliability cuts in both directions. More hardware provides redundancy and headroom against failures, which is a genuine benefit. But it also expands the surface area we must maintain, and a small team that spreads itself across more machines often ends up with worse, not better, operational reliability, because attention is finite. Improving utilisation typically involves building better observability and scheduling, and those systems improve reliability on the hardware we already trust. That said, if our current setup is a single point of failure with no failover, that is an argument for at least modest capacity expansion on resilience grounds alone, and I would want us to check that explicitly before finalising anything.

The opportunity cost question is the one I find most persuasive. Every pound and every engineering-week spent on procurement is a week not spent on the model improvements, evaluation harnesses, and product work that actually differentiate us. Hardware is a commodity; what we build on top of it is not. Moreover, the hardware market is moving quickly enough that deferring a purchase by even one quarter likely gets us more capability per pound. Waiting is not free—there is a cost to constrained capacity today—but it is a cost we can measure against the alternative.

Finally, reversibility. Utilisation work is almost entirely reversible or at least neutral: if we over-batch and latency suffers, we tune it back; if quantisation degrades quality on some task, we revert that model. A hardware purchase is a one-way door. When a decision is asymmetric like this, the burden of proof should sit with the irreversible option, and I do not think the evidence currently clears that bar.

I want to be honest about uncertainty. I do not have precise figures for our current utilisation, and my sense that we are leaving significant headroom on the table is informed but not measured. It is possible that demand is genuinely at capacity and utilisation work buys us only weeks. That is why the recommendation includes a concrete checkpoint: instrument the hardware, measure real utilisation and latency percentiles, implement the scheduling and batching improvements, and reconvene in one quarter with data. If the numbers show sustained saturation, I will support the purchase without further argument.

In short: measure first, optimise second, buy third. That ordering respects our budget, our latency needs, our reliability posture, and the fact that one of these decisions can be undone and the other cannot.

# Memo: On Buying More AI Hardware Versus Using What We Have

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** Capacity decision for local AI compute

We've been asked to decide whether to purchase additional local AI hardware or to invest our limited engineering time in improving utilisation of the machines we already own. This memo lays out the case for each path and closes with a recommendation. I want to be upfront that the recommendation rests on estimates rather than measurements, and I'll flag where our data is weakest.

Let's start with the facts we're reasonably confident about. Our current fleet runs inference workloads for internal tooling, model experimentation, and a small number of customer-adjacent services. Peak demand has grown steadily, and we occasionally queue jobs during business hours. At the same time, our own sampling suggests average GPU utilisation sits well below what the hardware can sustain. We are, in other words, buying capacity we already own but fail to extract. That gap is the crux of the decision.

The purchase path is seductive because it is simple. New hardware arrives, capacity roughly doubles, and the queueing problem disappears for perhaps a year. But the cost is not just the capital outlay. There is rack space, power, cooling, and the ongoing maintenance burden on a team that is already stretched. There is also depreciation: AI accelerators lose value quickly as newer generations ship, so a purchase made today is worth considerably less in eighteen months. And critically, a purchase does nothing to fix the underlying scheduling and batching inefficiencies that created the utilisation gap. If we buy hardware to paper over poor utilisation, we will eventually face the same decision again, at a higher baseline cost.

The utilisation path is harder but more durable. Better job scheduling, batching of small inference requests, off-peak training runs, and reclaiming idle capacity from stale experiments could plausibly recover a large fraction of the headroom we need. The costs here are mostly in engineering time, which is our scarcest resource. Every week spent tuning schedulers is a week not spent on product work, and that opportunity cost is real and easy to underestimate. The work is also less predictable: we believe we can recover meaningful capacity, but we haven't measured it rigorously, and there's a chance the gap is smaller than our sampling suggests, or that the workloads are genuinely bursty in ways that scheduling cannot smooth.

Latency considerations cut in both directions. Adding hardware reduces contention and therefore tail latency for interactive workloads, which matters for the services with users waiting on responses. Utilisation improvements, by contrast, can sometimes increase latency for individual jobs if we pack work more aggressively. However, smarter batching often improves throughput per request without materially hurting tail latency, so this is not a clean win for the purchase path. We should measure latency under a packed schedule before assuming the trade-off is severe.

On reliability, the purchase path adds failure domains and maintenance surface, but also redundancy; if one node fails today, we feel it acutely. The utilisation path adds no new hardware risk but concentrates more critical work onto existing machines, which are aging. Neither path is clearly safer, though new hardware does come with warranties and vendor support that our current fleet increasingly lacks.

Reversibility deserves particular weight. A hardware purchase is largely irreversible: once the capital is spent, we cannot easily unwind it, and resale value for used accelerators is poor. The utilisation work, by contrast, is highly reversible and composable. If scheduling improvements recover less capacity than hoped, we can still buy hardware afterwards, and the engineering investment will make whatever fleet we own run better. If the improvements succeed, we may defer the purchase by a year or more, which is itself valuable given how quickly the hardware landscape is shifting. Waiting also preserves optionality on newer, more efficient accelerators that are expected to reach the market within our planning horizon.

My recommendation is therefore to invest in utilisation first, with a defined checkpoint. We should spend roughly one quarter on scheduling, batching, and reclaiming idle capacity, instrument the fleet properly so we have real utilisation data rather than samples, and revisit the purchase decision at the end of that period with clear thresholds: if measured utilisation after improvements still cannot absorb projected demand, we buy, and we buy with better information and a well-tuned fleet to absorb the new capacity.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. Our utilisation estimates come from limited sampling and could be off in either direction. Demand growth could accelerate beyond what any efficiency work absorbs. If either of those proves true, the checkpoint lets us pivot to purchase quickly, and we should pre-approve a procurement path now so the checkpoint doesn't become a bottleneck. The plan costs us one quarter of optionality; the alternative risks spending significant capital to solve a problem we may already have the capacity to solve.

**Memo: Local AI Hardware — Purchase vs. Utilisation**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** [Your name]
**Date:** [Date]
**Re:** Recommendation on proposed GPU capacity expansion

---

Over the past several weeks we have discussed whether to purchase additional local AI hardware or to invest our limited engineering time in improving utilisation of the machines we already own. This memo lays out the tradeoffs as I see them, offers a recommendation, and flags the areas where I remain genuinely uncertain.

Let's start with the cost picture, because it frames everything else. The proposed purchase — two additional accelerator nodes plus the supporting networking and rack infrastructure — represents a capital commitment in the low six figures, with meaningful ongoing costs in power, cooling, and maintenance contracts. That is not a sum we can treat lightly given our current budget cycle. By contrast, improving utilisation costs us almost nothing in capital. Our current fleet runs at roughly 40 percent utilisation during business hours and considerably less overnight, which means we are, in a real sense, already paying for capacity we are not using. The cheapest capacity available to us is the capacity we have already bought.

That said, utilisation improvements are not free. They cost engineering time, and that time has an opportunity cost. The two engineers who would lead a scheduling and batching overhaul are the same people we are counting on to ship the inference optimisation work that directly supports our product roadmap. If we spend a quarter chasing utilisation percentage points, we may find we have optimised our infrastructure while our competitors optimised their product. This is the crux of the decision: it is not hardware versus nothing, it is hardware versus everything else those hours could accomplish.

Latency considerations cut in both directions. Adding nodes would give us headroom to run more workloads concurrently without contention, which would improve tail latencies for interactive requests. But our worst latency offenders today are not caused by raw capacity shortages — they are caused by poor batching decisions and workloads that should never have been co-located sharing the same devices. Fixing those problems improves latency for every workload we run, including future ones, whereas adding hardware merely dilutes the problem across a larger fleet. If we buy first and optimise later, we risk building habits and architectures that assume abundant capacity and are expensive to unwind.

Reliability deserves its own consideration. More hardware means more failure domains, more firmware drift, more spares to stock, and more surface area for the intermittent faults that consume on-call time. Our current fleet is well understood; we know its failure modes and we have runbooks for them. New hardware, particularly from a vendor we have less operational experience with, introduces a burn-in period during which reliability is typically worse, not better. There is also a supply-chain dimension: lead times on accelerator hardware remain volatile, and committing to a purchase now locks us into a specific generation of silicon at a moment when the hardware landscape is shifting quickly.

Which brings me to reversibility, the factor I weight most heavily. Buying hardware is a largely irreversible decision. Once purchased, the capital is sunk, the machines depreciate, and if our workload projections prove wrong, we are left reselling equipment at a steep discount or letting it idle. Improving utilisation, by contrast, is almost entirely reversible and compounding. Better scheduling, quota enforcement, and workload isolation make us more efficient regardless of what hardware we eventually run on. If, after three to six months of disciplined utilisation work, we still face genuine capacity shortfalls, we can make the purchase decision then — with better data on real demand, clearer visibility into vendor roadmaps, and no loss of optionality. The reverse ordering does not hold: hardware bought prematurely cannot be un-bought.

My recommendation, then, is to defer the purchase for two quarters and commit to a focused utilisation effort: implementing proper gang scheduling and preemption, enforcing fair-share quotas so no single team can monopolise the fleet, and right-sizing the batch jobs that currently request far more than they need. I would set a concrete trigger for revisiting the purchase — for example, sustained utilisation above 80 percent with unmet demand in the queue — so this becomes a data-driven decision rather than a deferred one.

I want to be honest about the uncertainties. Our demand forecast could be badly wrong; if a major customer commitment lands, we may need capacity faster than utilisation work can deliver, and we should pre-qualify a rental or cloud-bursting option as a bridge. It is also possible that utilisation work stalls for organisational reasons — quota enforcement is politically harder than it sounds. And I acknowledge that deferring has its own cost: engineers may chafe at constraints, and some friction is real.

On balance, though, the asymmetry is decisive. Utilisation work is cheap, reversible, and improves everything downstream; the hardware purchase is expensive, irreversible, and can still happen later if justified. Let's do the cheap, reversible thing first.

Happy to discuss at Thursday's review.
